metadata.title: A Conflict-Free Replicated JSON Datatype
metadata.venue: IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems (TPDS)
metadata.abstract_summary: Gives an algorithm and formal semantics for a JSON-shaped CRDT — maps, lists, and ordered text nested arbitrarily — so that concurrent, uncoordinated edits from different replicas always converge to the same state with no updates silently lost, extending prior single-type CRDT research (registers, counters, sets) to the composite, nested document shape real applications actually use.

sections.heading: Bottom Line

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text: As the abstract states it (excerpted): many applications model their data in a general-purpose format such as JSON, but existing CRDT research addresses individual data types (registers, sets, counters) in isolation; the paper presents "an algorithm and formal semantics for a JSON data structure that automatically resolves concurrent modifications such that no updates are lost, and such that all replicas converge towards the same state (a conflict-free replicated datatype or CRDT)." The datatype supports arbitrarily nested maps, lists, and JSON primitives, plus a specialised approach for concurrent editing of ordered lists of characters (i.e., collaborative plain-text editing) as a special case of the general list type.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: An algorithmic and formal-semantics paper rather than an empirical one: the authors define the datatype's operations and merge function, then use formal proof techniques (the paper states the semantics are formally specified and the convergence properties proved, consistent with the CRDT literature's standard approach of proving commutativity/associativity/idempotence of the merge operation directly rather than testing it empirically). This is the theoretical register the [[Kleppmann et al., 2019 - Local-first software]] essay's own further-reading list points to when it cites "Martin Kleppmann's Convergence vs Consensus" and the Shapiro et al. CRDT survey — this paper is the primary, formal counterpart to that essay's popular framing.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- Published in a peer-reviewed venue (IEEE TPDS, 2017; DOI 10.1109/TPDS.2017.2697382) after two prior arXiv revisions (August 2016, March 2017), which is a stronger evidentiary bar than a preprint or blog post — the reason this note exists in the paper layer rather than being folded into a resource note's Reading Notes.
- As a formal-semantics paper, its evidence is proof, not measurement: it does not report benchmark numbers, production deployment data, or a comparison against alternative JSON CRDT designs at scale. Any performance or real-world-robustness claim belongs to the implementations (e.g. Automerge) that build on this design, not to this paper itself.
- This paper's own text, read directly, does **not** name Automerge. The link between the two is drawn by the 2019 Ink & Switch essay, which states Automerge "is based on our earlier research on JSON CRDTs" — a claim made by the same lead author (Kleppmann) about the same specific technical contribution (a JSON CRDT) this paper delivers. This note records that link as a well-evidenced but external inference, not as a fact asserted inside this paper's own text, and lists it in `implemented_by` on that basis.
